title: Exam Study Expert: ace your exams with the science of learning
author: William Wadsworth
description: Don't work harder, work smarter: how to study effectively and get the grades of your dreams. Cambridge-trained psychologist and learning science researcher William Wadsworth shares review strategies, memory techniques, and exam preparation tips.

episodes.title: 226: "Remember, It's Only An Exam": Keeping Your Cool In Exam Season
episodes.summary: William shares five mental reframes that reduce exam stress and help you perform under pressure, so you can revise with focus and walk into the exam room calmer and more in control.

episodes.title: 225: Handling Exam Pressure: High Performance Secrets With Dr Brian Hite
episodes.summary: Dr Brian Hite, a former stuntman turned sports psychologist, shares four stages of performance and real-time calming tools for high-stakes exam situations.

episodes.title: 224: "The Easy Button" For Exam Season Success
episodes.summary: Specific strategies to reduce short-term pressure and free up time for focused studying during a demanding exam season.

episodes.title: 223: Perfectionism, Self-Compassion and Making Progress - with Dr Tara Cousineau
episodes.summary: Harvard-trained psychologist Dr Tara Cousineau unpacks what triggers perfectionism and teaches self-compassion skills that balance ambition with wellbeing.

episodes.title: 222: Eating Your Frogs In The Final Weeks Before An Exam
episodes.summary: One guiding question for prioritising difficult material in the final weeks: treat resistance as a signal to tackle the hard content first.

episodes.title: 221: Your Emotional Toolkit for Academic Stress - with Dr Jennifer Veilleux
episodes.summary: Clinical psychologist Dr Jennifer Veilleux shares research-backed emotional regulation strategies for stress, anxiety, and procrastination across academic life.

articles.question: How do you stay calm during exam season?
articles.metaDescription: Psychologist William Wadsworth of Exam Study Expert shares five mental reframes that take the pressure off exams, from knowing your real target to having a Plan B.
articles.intro: Mostly by changing how you think about the exam, not by trying harder to relax. William Wadsworth, the psychologist behind the Exam Study Expert podcast, offers five mental reframes for exam season: work out what mark you actually need, have a Plan B, run your own race, treat the exam as a game with rules, and remember it's only an exam. Each one takes a bit of weight off, and together they make it a lot easier to revise well and perform on the day.

sections.heading: Work out the mark you actually need
sections.body:
William's first reframe is arithmetic. Most students revise as if they need every mark, but almost nobody does. If your target is 75 percent, you can drop one mark in four and still hit it. If you need a pass, the margin is even wider.

That's not an excuse to slack off. It's a permission slip to stop chasing total mastery of every topic. Goals are useful because they give your revision drive and focus, but a goal of perfection does the opposite: it makes every gap feel like a crisis. Knowing your real target lets you prioritise the material that matters most and accept that some corners won't be fully covered.

quote.text: Goals are good because they give us drive and focus in our exam prep.
quote.speaker: William Wadsworth

sections.heading: Know your Plan B, then stop thinking about it
sections.body:
The second reframe is to admit that a backup exists. Retakes, reapplying next year, an alternative course or route. William's point is that when you've named your Plan B, Plan A stops feeling like the only thing standing between you and disaster.

The paradox he describes is that easing your grip on the outcome usually improves it. A student who believes everything hinges on this one paper walks in tight and anxious. A student who knows there's another route if it goes wrong can breathe, think, and actually show what they know.

quote.text: When we take that intense pressure off your shoulders a little bit, we can breathe again.
quote.speaker: William Wadsworth

sections.heading: Run your own race
sections.body:
Exam season is full of comparison. Who's done more past papers, who's revised which topic, who says the exam is going to be brutal. William's third reframe is to opt out of the pack.

Practically, that means limiting conversations about revision with the people who wind you up, staying off the group chat the night before, and measuring yourself against your own plan rather than someone else's. Your job is to use your time well and make the best progress you can with the hours you have. What everyone else is doing is noise.

quote.text: Focus on using your time well, doing what makes sense to you, making the best progress.
quote.speaker: William Wadsworth

sections.heading: Treat the exam as a game with rules
sections.body:
Plenty of students resent exams. They think the format is unfair, the content is pointless, or the whole system is broken. William doesn't argue with any of that. He just points out that the exam in front of you is still the one you have to sit.

His fourth reframe is to park the philosophical objections and play the game to win. See the rubric, the mark scheme, and the timing as rules of a game, and get good at the game. He also suggests looking for the underlying skills the process builds, like problem solving, memorisation, and resilience, which have value long after the exam itself is forgotten.

quote.text: We need to set aside any philosophical disagreements with the exam, almost see the exam as a game.
quote.speaker: William Wadsworth

sections.heading: It's only an exam
sections.body:
The last reframe gives the episode its title. An exam measures a narrow slice of what you know on one day. It doesn't measure your kindness, your creativity, your friendships, or anything else that makes you who you are.

William is careful not to say exams don't matter. They do, and that's why you're preparing. But keeping them in proportion is part of preparing well. When the result feels like a verdict on your worth as a person, the anxiety becomes unmanageable. When it's one assessment among many things in a full life, you can take it seriously without being crushed by it.

quote.text: Don't lose sight of the fact that exams don't define who you are.
quote.speaker: William Wadsworth

keyTakeaways: Calculate the mark you actually need; the margin for error is usually bigger than you think.
Name your Plan B so Plan A stops feeling like everything, which usually improves performance.
Stop comparing revision with peers and limit anxiety-raising conversations before exams.
Set aside objections to the exam format and play the game to win, using the mark scheme as the rules.
Keep the exam in proportion: it measures one thing on one day, not who you are.

faq.q: Does being less stressed actually improve exam results?
faq.a: William's view is yes. Intense pressure makes it harder to think and recall, so taking some of the weight off, for example by having a Plan B, tends to help you perform better on the day.

faq.q: Should I avoid talking to friends about revision?
faq.a: Not entirely, but be selective. If certain conversations or group chats raise your anxiety about what everyone else is doing, William suggests limiting them and focusing on your own plan.

faq.q: What if I think the exam is unfair or pointless?
faq.a: William says to park that for now. It's still the exam you have to take, so treat it as a game with fixed rules, learn the rules, and play to win.
